Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: Eleanor remembered the Tuesday afternoon in October with a clarity that never faded, though the days leading up to it slipped through her grasp. She had been in the passenger seat while Robert navigated the familiar stretch of Route 9 when a truck swerved across the median. The sound was immediate and shattering, a brutal crunch of metal folding into itself that echoed long after the engines cut out. When she turned her head, she saw his hands still resting on the wheel, the windshield spiderwebbed, and the sharp, acrid scent of burnt rubber and spilled gasoline hanging in the air. That specific smell would later return unbidden, sometimes when a neighbor trimmed a hedge nearby, sometimes when she passed a service station, instantly dragging her back to the suffocating heat of that cab. In the months that followed, Eleanor found herself unable to sit with the memory deliberately. Every time she tried to trace what happened next, her mind would go blank, as though a heavy door had swung shut. Yet the memory would ambush her without warning—a flicker of sunlight on shattered glass, the distant wail of a siren—forcing the full, unvarnished scene back into her awareness. The days after the hospital marked a quiet unraveling. Eleanor stopped driving past the highway on purpose, and when news channels showed footage of mangled cars on the shoulder, she turned the television off before the impact could register. The anniversary of October thirteenth arrived like a physical weight. She spent the morning pacing the kitchen, her fingers testing the deadbolts on the front door, checking the living room windows, walking the perimeter, and then returning to the locks again. Each click of the latch was a small anchor, but it never quite held. At night, the stillness of the bedroom worked against her. She lay awake for hours, watching the ceiling fan cut through the dark, certain that if she drifted off, the cab would crush down around her. What frightened her most was the suddenness of her own body’s response. When her neighbor rushed to the porch in the morning to retrieve a dropped newspaper, Eleanor flinched so violently she knocked over a coffee mug, her heart hammering as if she were still bracing for impact. She had come to believe that the everyday world was fundamentally unpredictable, and that any abrupt shift could trigger the exact sequence of events that had already cost her so much. As an unemployed woman navigating her days alone, Eleanor spent her hours in the home office, now a quiet reading room, avoiding the outside world. By the third winter, the habits she had built around the accident had settled into her routine. One afternoon in late March, she stepped onto the back porch for coffee. An ambulance passed slowly down her street with its lights off, heading toward a different house entirely. Eleanor froze, the familiar scent of antiseptic and burnt metal rising in her throat. She turned and retreated inside, locking the door behind her, knowing that the distance between safety and collapse was thinner than she had ever imagined. She no longer visited the community center where she used to meet friends, preferring the controlled silence of her own walls to the unpredictable rhythm of public life. It was the approaching anniversary that finally pushed Eleanor to pick up the phone. She had hoped that time would soften the edges of the event, but the intrusions had grown sharper, and the exhaustion of constant vigilance was leaving her hollow. She sat on her sofa, staring at the clinic brochure, wondering if she could learn to stop scanning every room for exits, if she could let herself rest without waiting for the next impact. Most of all, she was terrified that she was losing herself to the past, that the woman who used to love gardenias and Sunday crosswords was being swallowed by the smell of smoke and the sound of crumpling steel. She dialed the number on the brochure, hoping someone could help her remember that October afternoon without drowning in it.
